item.title: Nature Biotechnology: Re-evaluating the site-directed nuclease classification as a regulatory trigger for genome-edited plant products
item.description: Nature Biotechnology, Published online: 05 March 2026; doi:10.1038/s41587-026-03028-0 Site-directed nuclease (SDN) classification into SDN-1, SDN-2 and SDN-3 outcomes is used for regulating genome-edited plant products in some countries. This reductive categorization system fails to cover the breadth of genome editing technologies developed over the past decade and their rapidly approaching commercial use. Here, we argue that, in the context of plant breeding, regulations should focus on the characteristics of the genome editing outcome, rather than specific methods used in the development process. Such a science-based, outcome-focused regulatory approach would future-proof the risk-proportionate oversight of plant breeding innovations and enable a more efficient delivery of improved crop varieties amidst growing concerns of climate change and evolving pests and diseases.

item.title: Nature Methods: Large-scale library of 3D ant images captured with synchrotron X-ray microtomography
item.description: Nature Methods, Published online: 05 March 2026; doi:10.1038/s41592-026-03004-1 This study introduces an unprecedented resource of thousands of 3D images representing the diversity of an ecologically dominant group of insects: ants. These data were generated using high-throughput synchrotron X-ray microtomography, which opens a pathway to scalable digitization of the vast diversity of invertebrate life.

item.title: Nature Methods: High-throughput phenomics of global ant biodiversity
item.description: Nature Methods, Published online: 05 March 2026; doi:10.1038/s41592-026-03005-0 Antscan is a publicly accessible database of synchrotron X-ray CT images of ants. The database covers almost 800 species from more than 200 genera and is coordinated with genome sequencing projects that will enable integrative analyses.

item.title: Nature Biotechnology: Quantification and transcriptome profiling reveal abundant, dynamic and translatable dephospho-CoA-capped RNAs
item.description: Nature Biotechnology, Published online: 04 March 2026; doi:10.1038/s41587-026-03040-4 An enzyme that specifically recognizes dephospho-CoA (dpCoA)-capped RNAs is used to quantify dpCoA-RNAs in cells.

item.title: Nature Methods: It’s a colorful pangenome world
item.description: Nature Methods, Published online: 04 March 2026; doi:10.1038/s41592-026-03021-0 A pangenome can reveal the spectrum of genome variation within a species. The toolbox for working with pangenomes is filling up.

item.title: Nature Methods: A unified framework for multiomics deconvolution
item.description: Nature Methods, Published online: 02 March 2026; doi:10.1038/s41592-026-03008-x The new algorithm DECODE transcends the limitations of omics-specific methods, and provides a unified framework for the deconvolution of transcriptomic, proteomic and metabolomic datasets.

item.title: Nature Methods: DECODE: deep learning-based common deconvolution framework for various omics data
item.description: Nature Methods, Published online: 02 March 2026; doi:10.1038/s41592-026-03007-y DECODE is a universal deconvolution framework for both cell types and cell states that can be applied to transcriptomic, proteomic and metabolomic data.

item.title: Nature Biotechnology: Considerations for the future of in vitro gametogenesis in fertility care
item.description: Nature Biotechnology, Published online: 26 February 2026; doi:10.1038/s41587-026-03034-2 The potential use of in vitro gametogenesis (IVG) as a reproductive technology could redefine parentage, including the possibility of bipaternal parentage, raising hopes for those who have infertility or desire reproductive autonomy. However, IVG is not yet feasible for human reproduction, and substantial hurdles must be overcome if it is to become a clinical reality. This Comment outlines the major technical limitations of IVG and argues for public engagement in shaping the future directions of IVG research.

item.title: Nature Methods: Next-generation multicolor indicators for in vivo imaging of norepinephrine
item.description: Nature Methods, Published online: 26 February 2026; doi:10.1038/s41592-026-03006-z Improved red and green indicators for norepinephrine and their characterization are reported. These indicators allow detection of norepinephrine release in awake behaving mice in dual-color fiber photometry and two-photon imaging applications.

item.title: Nature Biotechnology: Highly mutagenic continuous evolution in E . coli using a Φ29-based orthogonal replication system
item.description: Nature Biotechnology, Published online: 24 February 2026; doi:10.1038/s41587-025-02944-x Mutational rates of bacterial evolution are increased using an error-prone orthogonal system.

item.title: Nature Biotechnology: Agentic AI and the rise of in silico team science in biomedical research
item.description: Nature Biotechnology, Published online: 24 February 2026; doi:10.1038/s41587-026-03035-1 This study examines the emerging use of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) in biomedical research, highlighting the challenges and opportunities that may inform the design of agentic AI systems suitable for broad deployment.

item.title: Nature Biotechnology: Transposable elements in the dark genome
item.description: Nature Biotechnology, Published online: 23 February 2026; doi:10.1038/s41587-026-03012-8 Transposable elements (TEs), such as retrotransposons and endogenous retroviruses, are increasingly recognized for their important roles in genome function and impact on disease development. Residing mostly in the ‘dark genome’ — the part of the genome that does not encode proteins — TEs have long been difficult to study because of their repetitive nature. Recent technological advances are helping researchers overcome this issue, allowing them to identify how TEs contribute to disease development and discover novel targets for therapeutics. Despite this progress, the field still faces challenges. How can we translate this growing understanding of the dark genome into therapeutics? We asked experts in the field for their thoughts.

item.title: Nature Methods: Mentoring echoes down the generations
item.description: Nature Methods, Published online: 13 February 2026; doi:10.1038/s41592-026-03009-w As they train the next generation of scientists, some senior researchers share why they find mentoring fun and rewarding.
